questions.a: The protagonist is the first-person narrator ("eSa"), an educated, relatively privileged observer who encounters two children from a vaèkfo'okl community during a water crisis. questions.q: Compare the narrator's attitude toward the vaèkfo'okl old woman (thth) with his attitude toward the children. How does the difference expose his class consciousness?
questions.a: With thth, he engages in intellectual debate ("R;kx rks og gksrk--- mlh dk iQy feyrk gSA"), treating her as a sparring partner for abstract ideas. With the children, he acts on immediate physical need but draws a hard line when they return. The difference exposes that he respects the old woman's agency as a thinker but sees the children only as victims of a system he analyzes but does not dismantle. A wrong answer that says "he treats both kindly" ignores the power dynamic: he debates the elder, he rations the children.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrator's reliability. Does his self-awareness ("eSaus rks xk¡o osQ enjls dk Hkh eq¡g ugha ns[kkA") make him more or less credible as a witness to the water crisis? Justify.
questions.a: His admission of ignorance ("I have not even seen the faces of the children of the city") enhances credibility: it signals he knows the limits of his own experience. A reliable narrator in a realist text acknowledges partial vision. A student who claims "he is unreliable because he is biased" confuses subjectivity (inevitable in first-person) with unreliability (deliberate distortion). The narrator's bias is transparent; that is a strength, not a flaw.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the narrator's perspective the night after the final encounter, capturing his unresolved tension between "R;kx" (charity) and "cqokbZ" (systemic exchange).
questions.a: A strong entry will use first-person, reference specific images (the empty pot, thth's laughter, the children's silence), and end with an open question, not a resolution. Example: "The pot is dry. Thth's laugh echoes — 'igys [kqn nks rc nsork...' — and I have no answer. I gave water; I gave a bucket. Tonight the well is empty again. Is charity just a slower violence? I return to my books, but the thirst remains." A weak entry resolves the tension ("I will dig a well tomorrow") or uses third-person, missing the protagonist's voice.
